https://www.liverpoolecho.co.uk/whats-on.text: Two friends from Hungary are attempting to bring a piece of their childhood to Liverpool in what would be a first for the city. Miklos Olah and Daniel Weisz are on the path to creating the first authentic Hungarian bakery, which would feature theatre-style operations and recipes from their homeland. Miklos moved to Liverpool ten years ago from Budapest , with the city becoming a permanent home for his family. Daniel is a long‑time friend from the same area, who has supported the project from the beginning, helping with brand development, product refinement and operational planning. Taking inspiration from their childhood roots , they hopes to create a bakery that offers authentic Hungarian chimney cakes in a modern, theatre‑style operation where everything is made rom scratch in front of customers. Miklos told the ECHO : "Chimney cake is part of our childhood, a tradition we grew up with. We remember it from festivals, family gatherings, Christmas markets and weekend trips. The smell, the rolling of the dough and the caramelising sugar are childhood memories every Hungarian recognises instantly. "It’s a tradition passed down through families and perfected over generations. We’re not recreating chimney cake from a recipe - we’re bringing the real thing from our own culture. "The preparation happens fully in front of guests. The dough rolling, baking and caramelising is a theatre‑style moment. People don’t just receive a dessert, they watch it being made." The location of Buda&Pest is yet to be determined and will depend on capital, but Miklos hopes the roll out will begin in Kirkby , followed by Southport and into Liverpool city centre . A Crowdfunder has been launched with a target of £35,000 to open the first Buda&Pest bakery . Crowdfunder supporters will receive VIP soft‑launch access, pre‑order bundles and founder perks. The team will also attend pop-ups and markets around the region, with the menu focusing on chimney cakes at the early stages before branching out to classic Hungarian sweets, desserts, cakes and ice-cream. Miklos said: "We want to give back to the community that has given us so much over the past ten years. Liverpool helped us build a life, friendships and opportunities and this project is our way of contributing in return. "Our aim is to create local jobs, collaborate with Liverpool‑based businesses, and build a community around a product that every age group can enjoy. "We’ve received strong encouragement from across the region including Knowsley , Sefton and Southport as well as many private individuals who’ve followed the journey and offered help, advice and connections. "This early support is one of the reasons we chose Crowdfunder. We wanted the community to be involved from day one." Miklos hopes the concept takes off and expands across the city and UK. He added: "Liverpool has a strong food culture. We want people to take away the memory of the experience."

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Houthi armed forces patrol Sana’a over the weekend as the rebel group swept down the west coast of Yemen and seized the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait. Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Houthi armed forces patrol Sana’a over the weekend as the rebel group swept down the west coast of Yemen and seized the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait. Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty Images Strait of Hormuz Gulf states postpone strait of Hormuz talks with Iran as Yemen conflict intensifies Impasse comes amid growing Saudi anger with Tehran over Houthi advances and strikes on airbase and pipeline Oil prices rise after drone attacks shut down Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Mon 14 Sep 2026 08.22 EDT Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Gulf states have postponed a critical meeting with Iran on the future of the strait of Hormuz owing to a lack of Arab consensus and growing Saudi Arabian anger with Tehran for helping the Houthis loosen Riyadh’s grip in Yemen. The stalemate over the vital waterway came as Houthi rebels launched a fresh barrage of missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets. A Houthi military spokesperson claimed its forces had attacked the King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, hitting fighter-jet hangars, radar systems, runways and landing strips, ammunition depots and additional targets. Last week, Tehran-backed militias in Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to close a critical east-west pipeline that had been acting as a means for Riyadh to export oil after Iran effectively closed the strait of Hormuz. The closure of the pipeline, the postponement of the Hormuz meeting, and the Houthis’ seizure last week of Yemen’s Red Sea coast – which gave the group control over another vital waterway, the Bab al-Mandab strait – combined to drive up oil prices above $108 a barrel on Monday. View image in fullscreen A screengrab of video released by the Houthi authorities shows fighters during an offensive in the port city of Mocha, Yemen. Photograph: Houthi Military Media Center Handout/EPA Also on Monday, the Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman, held urgent discussions with the US ⁠Central Command chief ⁠Adm ​Brad Cooper in Jeddah to discuss “the latest developments in the region”, according to Saudi media. Sources told US media last week that the Saudi de facto ruler had sought military assistance ‌from Donald Trump to help fight the Houthis . So far the US has provided only logistical and intelligence backing, Middle East map 14 September The Gulf Cooperation Council-Iran meeting was postponed at the last minute, deferring a proposed agreement on a new temporary route for commercial shipping when the strait of Hormuz is reopened. In a statement, Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, said the meeting had been delayed in the interests of consensus. “We remain committed to fostering dialogue that supports stability and lasting co-operation in our region,” he wrote on X. He gave no further details. The meeting would not have led to the immediate opening of the strait, since Tehran has set a series of other preconditions: including requiring the US to lift a blockade of Iran’s oil ports, the handing over of many frozen Iranian assets and a ceasefire in Lebanon. But it would have been the first meeting between Iran and the main GCC member countries for two years. The planned agreement on a temporary route for ships to use would have formalised Iran’s control of the strait, since the entry route would have been entirely in Iranian waters. Washington has not expressed publicly an opinion over the proposed deal, and some of Trump’s recent social media posts – claiming full US control of the strait – seemed to bear little relationship with what shipping companies have been reporting. The atmosphere surrounding the meeting, in preparation for weeks, had been rapidly souring because of the advance by the Houthis in Yemen and the drone attack on the Saudi pipeline by an Iran-backed Shia militia in Iraq. Vantor Technologies released high-resolution satellite images showing the damage to the east-west pipeline pumping station near Al Mesba’ah, Saudi Arabia. The station appears to be almost completely destroyed. View image in fullscreen A satellite shows damage to a pumping station along the east-west pipeline near Al Mesaba’ah, Saudi Arabia. Photograph: Satellite image ©2026 Vantor/AFP/Getty Images Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson denied any Iranian involvement in the pipeline attack, or on events in Yemen. US military bases throughout the Gulf have been attacked by Iran in response to the Iran war. Saudi Arabia, which backs the UN-recognised Yemeni government based in Aden, is trying to regain the initiative after Houthi forces swept down the west coast of Yemen from the port of Hodeidah last week and seized the Bab al-Mandab strait, a narrow waterway that links the Red Sea with Asia and is viewed as second in strategic importance to the strait of Hormuz. It was claimed that a Saudi air bombardment was making it difficult for the Houthis to gain full control of the Yemen waterway or the strategic islands in the Red Sea. View image in fullscreen A commercial vessel anchored off Yemen’s coast at Bab al-Mandab. The Houthis leadership says it is seeking to block only Saudi-linked ships. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images The Houthi leadership says is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea but only Saudi-linked ships. It is also offering cut-price fees in the ports it controls on the west coast of Yemen in an effort to lure traffic away from the ports controlled by the Aden-based government in the south. It is widely accepted that Iran backs the Houthis, but the group also operates independently of Tehran. The rebels ultimate aim is to oust Saudi Arabia from the country, and take full control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has tried different tactics in handling the Houthis during the decade-long civil war in Yemen, including making concessions in the hope the highly ideological group would reach a power-sharing deal. The Yemen government said preliminary tolls indicated that 150 civilians had been killed and 200 others injured in the course of the recent Houthi advance. About 85,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN. https://www.dw.com/en/arctic-power-plays.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Matn Looking ahead: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and other European leaders gathered in Finland to discuss the future of the Arctic Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Known as the "Gateway to the Arctic ," the Finnish city of Rovaniemi sits directly on the Arctic Circle. Its forests are glowing in autumn colors as European leaders gather here at the invitation of Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to discuss a new EU strategy for the Arctic. Climate change and Russia’s war against Ukraine have thrust the High North into the center of European attention. "There is a high demand for concrete EU action in the Arctic," Orpo said. "Our security environment has changed fundamentally. The Arctic has emerged as a central arena of great power competition." The prime minister added that the Arctic's critical natural resources are also "attracting interest." A changing security environment in the High North The changing security environment was a central theme throughout the summit. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Russia is reopening former Soviet military bases in the region and conducting missile exercises in the High North. "We also see that China is increasingly more interested in the region, so we have to remain vigilant," Kallas said. The leaders gathered at Finland's northernmost air force base, looking up into a cloudless blue sky as Finnish fighter jets took to the air for a demonstration. Security has been placed at the heart of the discussions by Prime Minister Orpo. From Rovaniemi, Finland's Air Force monitors the skies along Europe's Arctic border with Russia ― 24/7. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who attended despite facing significant political pressure at home, described the region as increasingly important to Europe's security: "This region has become a geopolitical hotspot. Russia is building up its military capabilities here and… uses its presence for hybrid activities every day." Merz added that the Arctic is not only a security issue, but also offers major economic opportunities, particularly when it comes to critical raw materials. European leaders learned about Finnish fighter jets during the Arctic summit as well Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance Confrontation replaces cooperation "From the Putin era onwards, Russia has been developing its military capacities everywhere, but also in the Arctic," said Timo Koivurova of the Arctic Centre at the University of Lapland. For years Western countries still continued cooperating with Moscow on scientific research and climate issues. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine brought that era to an end. Finland and Sweden joined NATO as a direct consequence of the war. Finland's 1,340-kilometer border with Russia is now also a NATO border, fundamentally changing the security landscape in northern Europe. The European Commission plans to update its 2021 Arctic Strategy as early as October 2026. The summit's joint declaration calls for greater investment in military mobility, cross-border connectivity and critical infrastructure in the EU's northernmost regions, including transport links, digital networks and satellite technologies. Koivurova said that Russia's current focus on Ukraine and that war takes its military capacities. "But obviously when that war is over, and someday it will be over, there will be a lot of investments from Russia, very likely also in the northern regions, because they are so important for its overall security," Koivurova told DW. The United States as an additional stress factor The Arctic is also being affected by tensions among Western partners, Koivurova said. In particular, he argued that US President Donald Trump's proposals regarding Canada and Greenland have strained cooperation among Arctic allies. "Trump's proposal to have Canada as the 51st state of the United States, or the purchase of Greenland , these are really major problems for the cooperative relations between the western Arctic states," Koivurova said. "That is a kind of additional stress factor for Arctic governance cooperation." Veteran Arctic observer Markku Heikkila believes the region is increasingly divided. "In my opinion, [the] Arctic is now slowly dividing into three parts," Heikkilä told DW. He said Russia forms one bloc, while countries such as EU member states, Norway, Iceland and Canada continue to defend a rules-based international order, climate action and Indigenous rights. "Officially the position of the USA is now very much different from what it used to be," said Heikkila. Inside NATO's Arctic operation preparing for a Russia crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Climate change is transforming the Arctic At the same time, climate change is reshaping the Arctic faster than any other region on Earth. Scientists expect the central Arctic Ocean to become largely ice-free during summer sometime around 2040 and 2050. As sea ice retreats, the region is gaining strategic importance with new shipping routes and significantly shortening distances between major trading centers, creating new economic and geopolitical opportunities, says Koivurova. Yet climate policy has become another source of disagreement between the United States and many of its Arctic partners. "Climate change is, of course, a hugely important thing in the Arctic. It's warming four times the rate as compared to the global average. So everything we do in the Arctic nowadays, one way or the other, is related to climate change," Koivurova said. He added that the Trump administration's approach has had a significant impact on international cooperation, including within the Arctic Council: "The US is torpedoing any mention of climate change at the moment. So that was certainly a big, big change." Orpo: 'We should strengthen Arctic resilience' At the close of the summit, Prime Minister Orpo called for greater investment to strengthen the region's resilience. "We should strengthen Arctic resilience by strategic investments in Arctic infrastructure, dual use transport networks, critical raw materials, icebreaking and technological innovation," Orpo said. Rovaniemi is known worldwide as the hometown of Santa Claus. Not far from the "Arktikum" museum and science center where the leaders met lies "Santa Claus Village." It's home to the official Santa Claus Post Office, which remains open year-round. Visitors can also meet Santa himself. Whether any of the summit participants paid him a visit ― and if so, what they wished for ― remains unknown. https://www.theregister.com/columnists/2.text: REG AD columnists Big AI's content problem: Take the work, keep the money OPINION The more we learn about how AI does business, the more unfair it looks Steven J. Vaughan-Nichols Steven J. Vaughan-Nichols Published sun 27 Sep 2026 // 10:35 UTC Make us preferred on Google READ MORE Microsoft leans on open weight model from Chinese AI lab to challenge Jev 19 hours ago Microsoft 365 subscribers set to lose up to 4 TB of OneDrive storage 1 day ago Anthropic asks users to stop being mean to Claude 1 day ago Microsoft and Anthropic play invoice tennis with startup's $17,600 Claude bill 1 day ago India’s tech giants shrug off changes to USA’s skilled visa program 1 day ago Big AI has a problem. Its companies must ingest other people’s work. You know, books, news stories, photographs, code, websites, that one original meme you came up with, and practically everything else on the internet to train its large language models (LLMs). We all know that. We also know that AI companies hate paying for any of it, obeying the licenses attached to it, or, God forbid, sharing their revenue with the companies and people who created the work in the first place. Recently, Big AI's default way of doing business: "Take it now, argue about legality later," has become more in your face than ever. Look, for example, at the copyright fight between The New York Times and OpenAI and Microsoft . According to 404 Media ’s reporting on recently unsealed court documents - arguments from the plaintiffs that the court has not yet ruled on - Microsoft allegedly knew what it was doing when it was importing the internet willy-nilly . Microsoft's Director of Applied Science, Dr. Brent Hecht, was quoted in the news plaintiffs' 92-page combined brief as saying: the case was about “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions." Indeed, it was possibly the “largest theft of labor in human history,” he was quoted as saying in the summary judgment brief from the journalists' lawyers [PDF]. This, mind you, wasn't a comment by a member of the press; it was from a senior Microsoft staffer. REG AD Hecht wasn't the only one at Microsoft who commented. In an internal Microsoft policy document also quoted in the court papers, the authors admitted generative AI could “significantly disrupt the employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained [because] LLMs are a product that destroys its supply chain.” That, in turn, leads to model collapse . Ironically, AI is killing the content-creator goose that lays the gold eggs of worthwhile content. REG AD Judge Sidney H. Stein of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York has not yet issued a decision on the case. OpenAI and Microsoft are actively disputing the plaintiffs' allegations under a "fair use" defense. They contend that using public articles and books to train large language models helps push forward public knowledge, and isn't acting as a "unlawful economic market substitute". But the statements the documents cites are real. Big AI knows it needs the content. Some of the companies concerned don't give a damn; money now, worry later is their motto. Those who can look past the revenue numbers are well aware they're engaged in what Microsoft itself called a “doom loop” of AI content strategy in those unsealed court documents. Will that stop them? Nah. According to the filing [PDF], which refers to sworn deposition testimony of OpenAI’s own corporate representative, it also testified that its LLMs were happy to vacuum up other people's work even when a paywall nominally protected it. Its rep was quoted as saying they were unaware of “any effort to detect paywall content in its training datasets” or “to remove paywall content from its training datasets.” When OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman was told OpenAI could hack its way through the firewall, he responded, “ah, nice.” Whether or not these statements are found to be reflective of a wider attitude, similar attitudes prevail amongst Big AI. Such policies could eventually come back and bite the LLM makers; it's already affecting the market for journalism, fiction writing, graphics creation, anything that demands humans actually get paid for producing original work. Warsaw, Poland: A stylized interpretation of the ancient Egyptian god Thoth (also the self-styled tag of the artist), states: "Nie bój się niczego, bowiem wszystko jest twoim," translating to: "Fear nothing, for everything is yours." Pic credit: Anton Kustsinski/Shutterstock But Big AI just doesn't want to pay for it. That's not a side effect. It's the business model. Joe User couldn't care less. They just want a quick answer that sounds right. Some of them couldn't care less about getting the right answers. As for looking deeper to see if the information they're regurgitating is accurate, forget about it! As an OpenAI software engineer put it: “No matter how prominently we show the links, users won’t click.” Well, I click. That's a big reason why Perplexity is my AI of choice . It's not that it gives a more reliable answer. No, it's that, unlike most LLMs, Perplexity provides sources and links , and I check them before accepting what it tells me. But then I'm a journalist whose degrees are in history, where my professors drummed into me that you always - a lways - look at the primary sources. REG AD Big AI takes the same approach with its code generators. The US Ninth Circuit recently handed GitHub, Microsoft, and OpenAI a narrow win in the Doe v. GitHub lawsuit . The court ruled that the plaintiffs hadn't established a claim under one particular provision of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) , which concerns the removal or alteration of copyright-management information (CMI). In short, the court said that generating new code without including CMI is not necessarily the same thing as removing or altering copyright information from an existing work. Judge Eric Miller wrote: “One who creates a new work and fails to include CMI cannot be said to have ‘removed’ or ‘altered’ anything.” This ruling didn't establish that GitHub Copilot or any other coding model may train on every open source project without restriction. It didn't determine that copying source code into a training set is always fair use. It did not decide that generated code cannot infringe copyright. And it certainly did not repeal the GPL, Apache, BSD, MIT, or any other open-source license. After all, open source isn't a synonym for “do whatever you want with it.” It just seems that way when AI gets its hands on open source code. That's the problem with AI-generated code. A programmer who receives a Copilot suggestion is very unlikely to check whether the GPL covers the code, or whether Apache covers the snippet from a library. The developer certainly can't tell which license terms may apply to the code that just popped up from Opus 5.5 or GPT 6 . As the guy from OpenAI said, people don't click the links, and in AI-enabled programming pipelines, they don't even have the links anyway. An open source-savvy attorney friend of mine has a bigger worry than this narrow decision. He told me that what gives him "pause is a broader trend. There are multiple cases where parties are litigating open source licenses as contracts rather than as the IP / copyright licenses they were written to be. Contract theories let a plaintiff sidestep the questions copyright forces you to answer. 'Do you own the work? Is it protectable expression? Was it actually copied?'" He added: "Those questions are the foundation on which licenses are built. Open source licenses are grants of permission to use someone's intellectual property. If a case can't show that any intellectual property was owned or infringed, it's fair to ask whether enforcing the license as a bare contract supports open source licensing or quietly turns it into something else." With AI in the mix, this issue will eventually become one of those nasty IP matters developers hate, businesses want to avoid, but that courts must settle with expensive lawyers whose hourly rates worry even AI millionaires. After all, IP uncertainty isn't a minor paperwork issue. It is a supply-chain security and compliance problem. If you use AI-generated code, you may be importing unknown legal obligations into your software. If you are an open-source developer, your work may be used to improve a proprietary service that returns code without provenance, attribution, or meaningful reciprocity. And if you are a customer, you may be relying on software whose origins no one can fully explain. The Ninth Circuit ruling didn't solve any of that. We're in for a lot more open source litigation that will make SCO vs. the known Linux universe look like a kerfuffle over a parking ticket. REG AD Then there is the latest wrinkle: A federal antitrust lawsuit against Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Google . The plaintiffs allege the companies coordinated to slow the development of advanced AI systems. The lawsuit points to public statements from AI leaders all calling for coordination to “pace” frontier AI development over a single weekend. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has argued for industry-wide coordination to slow frontier development . OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk have also publicly expressed versions of the view that powerful AI systems need controls and careful deployment. On its face, that sounds sensible. AI safety is a real issue. Anyone who says otherwise has not been paying attention. But there's a huge difference between all big AI players agreeing among themselves on how quickly a market should develop. This looks like an awful lot like competitors deciding who gets to compete, what they get to build, and when they may build it. The Big AI companies all look like good guys while simultaneously strangling their smaller competitors. To mere mortals, this may sound like an open-and-shut case. It's not. Antitrust law requires evidence of an agreement and actual harm to competition; executives making similar public comments is not enough. The plaintiffs will need considerably more than quotes about AI safety or responsible development to win. Besides, if they do win, so what? What recently looked like huge antitrust wins has had its teeth pulled when it came to actually punishing the likes of Google and its ad business , or its earlier "lose the case, win the settlement" with Google Search . Do you see the pattern here? Big AI has effectively argued that copyright law, open source licenses, and competition rules shouldn't slow them down. When creators object, they are told that training is fair use. When developers object, they are told that generated code is new code. When competitors object, they are told security requires the largest companies to coordinate. Funny how the answer always seems to leave Big AI with the data, the market, and the money, isn't it? The central issue isn't whether AI should be allowed to develop. It will develop. The issue is whether the companies building it should be allowed to treat everyone else’s work as a free raw-material supply, then use the resulting products to take away the creators’ traffic, revenue, and bargaining power. Unless we stop Big AI now from this land grab with GPUs, only a handful of trillionaires will really benefit from AI, with the rest of us becoming serfs in a 21st-century post-technology feudal system. ® columnists microsoft ai openai anthropic Make us preferred on Google REG AD Two characters open up a world of typosquatting opportunities in Chromium browsers Attackers abusing rare Cyrillic and Latin letters to impersonate popular websites OPINION EC users should be afraid of a US kill switch - not some new software EU executive branch is building a sovereign backup with Element, not replacing Teams.
